<Rep. Terri A. Sewell>: My colleagues, cancer affects everyone. Today's mark-up represents a result of dedicated work towards one common goal: providing a coverage pathway for innovative cancer screenings.
This mark-up is of the utmost importance given the impact cancer continues to have upon our closest colleagues. A late-stage cancer diagnosis stole our nation's champion and our dear, John Lewis. Cancer diagnosed in late stage stole Speaker Mike Johnson's 63-year-old father from him just 3 days before he was sworn in. Last Congress, our colleague, Sheila Jackson Lee shared her diagnosis of pancreatic cancer. This Congress, we have already lost three colleagues, Congressmen Slyvester Turner, Raul Grijalva, and Gerald Connolly to the battle of cancer. Cancer, indeed, knows no bounds. It can and does affect everyone.
This fight against cancer is personal to me, a late-stage cancer diagnosis took the life of my mother--the namesake for this important legislation, Ms. Nancy Gardner Sewell. I want to thank our colleague Rep. Jodie Arrington for being a co-champion of this bill and for surprising and honoring me in naming the bill after my mother, Nancy Gardner Sewell.
Who was she? My mom was:
• A devout Christian who lived a life of
faith.
• An exemplary educator and librarian-media
specialist. She served in the Selma schools for 36
years, where she shaped minds and lifted up children.
As a librarian, she was a strong advocate of reading
and a champion of literacy initiating the Reading is
Fundamental (RIF) program in 1973 delivering books to
children throughout Alabama, Mississippi and Tennessee.
A program that still serves the kids in Selma-Dallas
County and Alabama's rural blackbelt.
• Nancy Sewell was a trailblazing civic
leader. She became the first African American woman
elected to Selma's City Council and served as an
inspirational role model for women in politics.
Her favorite saying was ``Bloom where you are planted''. You can make a difference right where you are. And she made a big difference in the lives of the many people she touched. My mother believed in community. She believed that knowledge mattered. She believed that no one should be left behind--she strove to build bridges and tear down walls of injustice. Her life's work was about service, about caring, about making sure people had what they needed to flourish.
My Mom represents one of the millions of people who have lost their battle to cancer, and my personal story represents one of the millions of loved ones who have had to endure such a horrible loss. It is our duty to do whatever we can to rid this nation of the scourge of cancer by giving coverage and access to the most vulnerable in our society. Therefore, I hope you will join me in supporting H.R. 842 the Nancy Gardner Sewell Medicare Multi-Cancer Early Detection Screening Coverage Act.
Currently, this bill has overwhelming bipartisan support in both chambers of Congress! 295 of our colleagues in the House of Representatives, and 62 in the Senate have signed on to cosponsor this legislation since its introduction in February!
I am also overwhelmed by the support this bill has earned from cancer advocacy groups-- such as the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network, the Prevent Cancer Foundation, the National Minority Quality Forum, The Association of Community Cancer Centers, Cancer Support Community, Fight Colorectal Cancer, Go2 for Lung Cancer, The National Grange, the Ovarian Cancer Research Alliance, and more than 600 advocacy organizations across the country which include more than a dozen organizations in my home state of Alabama!
Mr. Chairman, I would like to acknowledge and thank the patient advocates attending today's markup. I request unanimous consent to enter the 2025 letter of support from the Prevent Cancer Foundation listing every nationwide endorsing organizations of this legislation.
Like so many Americans, my mother received her diagnosis of pancreatic cancer after the cancer had already spread, making it harder to treat. New cancer screening tools have the potential to change this. Multi-cancer early detection tests can screen for dozens of cancers--such as pancreatic--for which we have not previously been able to screen. This means we can catch more cancers in their earlier stages, giving patients their best chance at beating the disease.
This year, more than 600,000 Americans will die from cancer. This number could easily be reduced with early detection tools! 66 is the median age for receiving a cancer diagnosis in the United States. This legislation serves to provide our seniors the opportunity to fight cancer earlier when it is less deadly. When there are steps we can take to reduce the suffering associated with cancer, it is our responsibility to do so.
For Congress today this means ensuring Americans have access to the most effective tools to help combat the disease. Medicare laws do not currently provide timely coverage of these technologies. It is our job to proactively ensure accessibility for those who need it most.
We must step in and create a pathway for coverage and access for early detection tests. That is exactly what the MCED bill does. Like similar legislation we have passed that create coverage pathways and access for mammography and colorectal screenings. This legislation will drive value in Medicare by reducing the significant costs attributed to advanced cancer care, and more importantly, it will save lives.
I am so thankful for the support this bill has received, both in Congress and amongst the cancer community. This bill passed unanimously out of this committee last Congress, and I pray we do so again today!
Our work is not done until this bill becomes law. Millions of Americans are counting on us.
Thank you.
Terri A. Sewell.
